microsoft-365-lifecycle-management.title: Configure the expiration policy for Microsoft 365 groups (Microsoft Entra ID)
microsoft-365-lifecycle-management.notes: Microsoft Entra offers an expiration policy that manages the lifecycle of Microsoft 365 groups automatically: groups in active use are renewed, unused ones are deleted, and deleted groups can be restored for a limited time. An organization can have only one such policy, scoped to all, selected or no Microsoft 365 groups, with at most 500 groups in the selected scope. The minimum group lifetime is 30 days. Renewal is driven by real activity in SharePoint, Outlook, Teams and Viva Engage; active groups typically renew about 35 days before expiry without any owner notice. If a group is not renewed, owners are notified 30 days, 15 days and 1 day before expiration, and the group is deleted one day after it expires. Restoration by an owner or administrator is possible within 30 days. Legal hold keeps the group mailbox, and retention policies keep content reachable for eDiscovery. Groups Administrators and User Administrators manage the policy, and Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licences are needed for the members of covered groups.

microsoft-app-advisor.title: Get personalized, fast recommendations for your Marketplace listing (Microsoft Marketplace blog)
microsoft-app-advisor.notes: Microsoft App Advisor includes a listing optimization feature that uses AI to review a publicly available Microsoft Marketplace listing and return personalized suggestions for improving it. The blog post describes it as free, available on demand and, at the time of writing, limited to the US. It targets software companies with a published, publicly visible offer; anyone in the organization can use it after signing in with a Partner Center account and picking an offer, and several listings can be scanned. Each listing is rated from 1 to 5 in six categories: value proposition, solution description, information quality, presentation, clarity and coherence, and grammar and style. The recommendations are said to draw on Marketplace best practices and on the experience of Microsoft Marketplace Rewards editors. Because the output is AI generated, the post advises reviewing every suggestion before publishing, then editing the listing in Partner Center, republishing and rescanning after about 24 hours to measure progress. Claimed benefits are better clarity, search discoverability and engagement.

microsoft-commerce-incentives.title: MCI engagements overview (Partner Center)
microsoft-commerce-incentives.notes: Microsoft Commerce Incentives (MCI) is the incentive program managed through the Incentives workspace of Partner Center. This documentation page covers the Engagements section, where partners handle earning opportunities grouped by solution area, check which of their enrolled locations are eligible, and manage customers and claims. Each engagement has a summary with partner and customer qualification criteria, proof of execution requirements, resource links and rates. The roles Incentives admin and Incentives user can work in this area. Customer claims move through consent steps (customer claimed, awaiting consent, consent received, rejected or declined) and review steps (draft, submitted, under review, partner action required, approved, rejected, disputed, rejected final, canceled), with deadlines set in the MCI program guide; claims left in draft too long expire. A claim for a partner activity and a use-or-consume claim for Claiming Partner of Record are added through different options. An eligibility page lists enrolled locations with their payee profile status. The page itself does not state funding amounts or explain the program in general terms.

microsoft-entra-kerberos.title: Microsoft Entra Kerberos authentication overview
microsoft-entra-kerberos.notes: Microsoft Entra Kerberos turns Microsoft Entra ID into a cloud Key Distribution Center for the Kerberos protocol, so users can reach cloud and on-premises Kerberos-protected resources. It works for hybrid identities (generally available) and cloud-only identities (preview), the latter for Azure Files, Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows authentication to Azure SQL Managed Instance. At sign-in on an Entra-joined or hybrid-joined device, Entra ID issues a Primary Refresh Token and a cloud ticket-granting ticket for the realm KERBEROS.MICROSOFTONLINE.COM; hybrid users also receive a partial ticket that a domain controller exchanges for a full one. Cloud tickets are used to request service tickets, for example for Azure Files, with authorization through Azure RBAC rather than NTFS ACLs. Scenarios include Windows Hello for Business cloud Kerberos trust, FIDO2 key sign-in and FSLogix profiles. Limits named on the page: guests and cross-tenant users are unsupported, MFA conflicts with Azure Files access, a ticket holds at most 1,010 group SIDs, only AES-256 is used, and the storage account password must be rotated every six months.

microsoft-graph-toolkit.title: Microsoft Graph Toolkit overview
microsoft-graph-toolkit.notes: The Microsoft Graph Toolkit is a collection of reusable, framework-agnostic web components plus authentication providers for building apps on Microsoft Graph. The components follow web standards, work in modern browsers and frameworks such as React, Angular and Vue, resemble Microsoft 365 experiences, and can be styled through CSS custom properties and templates. The page lists 18 components, among them Login, Agenda, Person, People picker, File list, Planner tasks, To Do, Teams Channel picker, Taxonomy picker and a generic Get component, and React versions are available. Six providers handle sign-in and token acquisition: Custom, Electron, MSAL2, Proxy, SharePoint and TeamsFx. Typical targets are web apps, Teams tabs, progressive web apps, Electron apps and SharePoint web parts. An important caution at the top of the page: the toolkit is deprecated, the retirement period began on 1 September 2025 and full retirement is planned for 28 August 2026, and Microsoft recommends moving to the Microsoft Graph SDKs or other supported Graph tools.

microsoft-sway.title: Microsoft Sway (Wikipedia)
microsoft-sway.notes: Microsoft Sway is a presentation program in the Microsoft 365 family in which a user with a Microsoft account combines text and media into a presentable website. Microsoft developed it in-house and launched it in 2014 as an invite-only preview that did not require an Office 365 subscription; general release followed in August 2015. Content can come from the device or from online sources such as Bing, OneDrive and YouTube, with built-in integrations for OneNote, Bing, other Sways, YouTube, Mixcloud and Infogram. Unlike older web design tools, Sway includes hosting: sites live on Microsoft servers, are tied to the Microsoft account and can be viewed and edited in a browser through Office on the web. A Windows 10 app arrived in August 2015, while the iOS app, previewed in October 2014, was discontinued in December 2018 because of low usage. There is no offline editing or viewing. The page notes that the Sway feature blog has not been updated since April 2017, and that by 2025 the service had largely moved to the cloud.microsoft domain.

microsoft365dsc.title: Microsoft365DSC (project site)
microsoft365dsc.notes: Microsoft365DSC is an open-source project hosted on GitHub that is led by Microsoft engineers and maintained by the community. Its idea is to manage the configuration of a Microsoft 365 tenant declaratively, with a single configuration file that can span many workloads; the site lists resources for areas such as Azure AD, Exchange, Intune, Teams, SharePoint, Security and Compliance, Power Platform, Defender and Sentinel. Four capabilities are highlighted. Change management: one declarative definition for all workloads supports automated change processes. Snapshots: the current configuration of an existing tenant can be exported. Drift detection: the tenant is monitored continuously for configuration changes, and a detected drift can be corrected, logged or reported to admins by email. Comparison: the configurations of two or more tenants can be compared with a report of the differences. The site also mentions that Microsoft opened a public preview of Tenant Configuration Management APIs in Microsoft Graph on 27 January 2026 and links to guidance on moving from Microsoft365DSC to them.

migration-coexistence.title: Microsoft 365 tenant-to-tenant migrations (planning overview)
migration-coexistence.notes: This Learn page is a planning overview for moving users and data from one Microsoft 365 tenant to another, for mergers, divestitures, consolidation of several tenants or internal reorganizations. It compares three approaches: multi-workload orchestrated migration with Migration Orchestrator, individual workload migration using the cross-tenant mailbox, OneDrive and SharePoint tools, and partner or third-party tools. For phased migrations in which users exist in both tenants for a while, the page names three coexistence topics to plan for: mail routing between the tenants, calendar free/busy sharing, and Teams federation for cross-tenant communication. It points elsewhere for configuration details. Dependencies it highlights are that Teams content relies on Exchange mailboxes, and that OneDrive and SharePoint share a permissions model, so they are best moved together. Further planning points are identity mapping (keep the UPN or issue a new one, domain transfers), sufficient licences in the target tenant, and timeline factors such as mailbox sizes, content volume, mailboxes on hold and network bandwidth.

migration-wave.title: Migration wave planning (Cloud Adoption Framework)
migration-wave.notes: Migration wave planning splits a large migration into smaller groups of workloads that move together, which lowers risk and complexity and lets the team learn from each wave. The page recommends planning iteratively: create learning cycles after every wave, run the current wave while planning the next, and keep later waves flexible and only define the next one in detail. Dependencies drive wave composition. Direct dependencies should move together, indirect ones may move together or separately, and business dependencies call for moving related workloads and reporting systems together; when unsure, group conservatively because splitting later is easier. Sequencing advice is to start with simpler, lower-risk workloads, move non-production before production, include one or two representative complex workloads in early waves, and leave critical systems until the process has proven itself. Prioritization weighs business value against effort. Timelines need buffer time, checkpoints at 25, 50 and 75 percent, cutovers in suitable windows with documented rollback, and comparison of planned against actual duration after each wave. Azure Boards and Azure Migrate are suggested tools.

model-gateway.title: Using a gateway in front of Foundry models (Azure Architecture Center)
model-gateway.notes: This Azure Architecture Center guide explains why and how to place a reverse-proxy gateway between applications and AI model APIs. Without one, every client has to implement retries, back-off, failover and governance itself. A gateway applies the gateway offloading pattern and can provide federated authentication, rate limiting per client or team, routing and load balancing across model deployments with health checks and circuit breaking, queue-based handling of low-priority requests, cross-model monitoring with usage attribution for chargeback or showback, response caching, and policy enforcement such as token limits, content safety and restriction of parameters. Direct access causes problems across reliability (HTTP 429 handling), security (shared keys, per-resource rather than per-deployment access), cost attribution and quota visibility. The guide also warns that a gateway is a decision with trade-offs: it can become a single point of failure, widens the attack surface, sees raw prompts and responses, adds latency and cost, and must support streaming. Options are the built-in Foundry AI gateway, Azure API Management (preferred, with llm-token-limit and related policies) or custom code.

mqtt-quality-of-service.title: Communicate with your IoT hub using the MQTT protocol (Azure IoT Hub)
mqtt-quality-of-service.notes: Azure IoT Hub supports MQTT version 3.1.1 on port 8883, or over WebSocket on port 443, and requires TLS; unencrypted MQTT on port 1883 is not supported. On quality of service, device SDKs connect with CleanSession set to 0 and use QoS 1 by default, which means delivery is acknowledged. QoS 0 can be configured for faster exchange, but it is fire and forget, with no guarantee and no acknowledgement. QoS 2 is not supported: if a device publishes with QoS 2, IoT Hub closes the connection, and if a device subscribes with QoS 2 the hub grants at most QoS 1. Other behaviours on the page: retained messages are not persisted, only one active MQTT connection per device ID is allowed, a device can subscribe to five topics at a time, wildcard topic filters beyond the documented ones are not allowed, the maximum message size is 256 KB, and keep-alive handling has a server-side cap of about 29.45 minutes. Cloud-to-device messages sent while a device is offline are delivered on reconnect only if the session persists. For a full broker the page points to Azure Event Grid MQTT.

multi-repo.title: Monorepo vs polyrepo (Nx documentation)
multi-repo.notes: This Nx knowledge-base article contrasts keeping many projects in one repository (monorepo) with splitting them across separate repositories (polyrepo, or multi-repo). The author argues that modern tooling has made large monorepos technically manageable, so the choice is mostly organizational. In a polyrepo, shared code is usually published as versioned packages, cross-project changes span several pull requests and releases, each repository has its own CI pipeline, access is controlled per repository, dependency versions tend to drift because no single policy applies, and teams keep autonomy over workflows and conventions. The article recommends a polyrepo when strict repository-level access control is needed or when teams share little code, with the cost of harder code sharing and repeated maintenance in every repository. It also describes a middle path of several monorepos split along real boundaries. For AI coding agents, it notes that agents can work across polyrepos but cannot see consumers of the code they change, so cross-repo work needs extra coordination; it names Polygraph, from the Nx team, as a way to supply cross-repo context.

multitenancy.title: Multitenancy (Wikipedia)
multitenancy.notes: Multitenancy is a software architecture in which one instance of an application runs on a server and serves several tenants, each a group of users with shared access and privileges. Every tenant gets its own share of the instance, including data, configuration, user management and functionality, in contrast to multi-instance designs. The page describes three ways to separate data: separate databases (strongest isolation, highest cost per tenant), a shared database with separate schemas, and a shared database with a shared schema where a tenant identifier column separates rows (cheapest but most demanding on application-level security). Deployment models are silo (dedicated resources), pool (shared resources, best economies of scale, but exposed to noisy neighbours) and bridge (a hybrid). Advantages include spreading overhead across customers, fewer licences and simpler release management. Disadvantages include scaling limits of a single instance, more complex development, stricter security testing, update risk affecting all tenants, and noisy-neighbour effects that can be reduced with rate limits and quotas. Customization usually covers branding, workflow, data model and access control.

n8n.title: n8n documentation
n8n.notes: The n8n documentation introduces n8n as a workflow automation tool that combines AI capabilities with business process automation, and describes it as fair-code licensed (the page gives no licence terms). Workflows are built from connected steps, and the docs link to guides on building a first workflow, flow logic, expressions for transforming data and understanding executions. Two ways to run it are listed: n8n Cloud, with a free trial and paid plans, and self-hosting, via a one-line setup, Docker Compose or deployment on a cloud provider. The landing page also highlights AI-related material: guides for connecting Claude Desktop, Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex CLI to the n8n MCP server, plus example workflows such as an AI agent chat and a workflow that scrapes and summarizes web pages with AI. Other examples cover creating an API endpoint and joining different datasets. The page is a documentation entry point rather than a detailed technical description, so node concepts and licence details are only reachable through its links.

named-entity-recognition.title: Named-entity recognition (Wikipedia)
named-entity-recognition.notes: Named-entity recognition (NER) is a subtask of information extraction that locates named entities in unstructured text and assigns each to a predefined category, so plain text becomes annotated text. Typical categories are person, organization, location, geopolitical entity, time, quantity, monetary value and percentage; published hierarchies range from 29 types with 64 subtypes (BBN) to about 200 subtypes. The task is usually split into detecting name spans and classifying them. Approaches include grammar-based rules (high precision, low recall, costly expert work), statistical models such as conditional random fields trained on annotated data, gazetteers of known names, and today mostly transformer-based token classification. Evaluation uses precision, recall and F1; the CoNLL variant demands exact span and type matches. Challenges listed are ambiguity (JFK as a person or an airport), metonymy, poor transfer between domains, noisy informal text, fine-grained types and annotation cost. The page also notes that linking mentions to Wikipedia pages (wikification) can be seen as an extremely fine-grained form of NER.

nearshoring.title: Nearshoring (Wikipedia)
nearshoring.notes: Nearshoring means outsourcing business work, especially IT work, to a company in a nearby country, often one sharing a border with the client. Closeness can be geographic, cultural, linguistic, economic or political, and it usually brings the same or a similar time zone, easier communication and frequent visits. The page contrasts it with offshoring, where work goes to a distant country mainly to save cost and where time differences, local labour law and weaker oversight are the challenges. Benefits listed are lower costs, access to skilled workers, easier management, more day-to-day oversight and cultural ties to the client's market. Drawbacks are that language and culture differences still cause friction and that building trust takes time. Regional examples: Western European clients use providers in countries such as Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary and the Czech Republic; US clients nearshore to Canada, Mexico and Latin America. Software development is the most common use, followed by call centres and business process outsourcing. The page credits the Mexican firm Softtek, which trademarked the term in 1997, with popularizing the concept.

network-file-system.title: Network File System (Wikipedia)
network-file-system.notes: The Network File System is a distributed file system protocol that Sun Microsystems developed in 1984 so that a client can access files over a network much as it would local storage. It is built on ONC RPC. Version 2 (RFC 1094, 1989) was the first released outside Sun and ran over UDP only with a stateless server; version 3 (RFC 1813, 1995) added 64-bit file sizes, asynchronous writes and TCP support; version 4 became stateful, required strong security through RPCSEC_GSS and used a single port, 2049, which simplified firewalls. Version 4.1 added clustered-server support including parallel NFS, and 4.2 (RFC 7862, 2016) added server-side copy, sparse files and labeled NFS. After Sun handed development to the IETF, all later versions are open standards specified in RFCs. Side protocols include the Network Lock Manager for locking. The page lists NFS support on many platforms, including Unix-like systems, Windows and OpenVMS, although some systems such as macOS and Windows default to SMB.

network-slicing.title: Network slicing (Wikipedia)
network-slicing.notes: Network slicing is an architecture that runs several separate virtual networks on one shared physical network, each slice being an isolated end-to-end network tailored to the requirements of a particular application. It matters for 5G because services such as mobile broadband, machine-to-machine communication in manufacturing and logistics, and smart cars have very different performance needs that a one-size-fits-all network cannot meet. Slicing relies on software-defined networking and network function virtualization. In the described business model an infrastructure provider leases resources to mobile virtual network operators, who deploy their own slices. The architecture has a service layer, a network function layer and an infrastructure layer, with a central slice controller that orchestrates and monitors slices. In the 5G core, control and user plane are separate, so user-plane functions can sit near the edge to cut latency; some functions such as AMF, UDM and NSSF are usually shared across slices. Isolation means one slice's load or attack should not affect another and slice-specific data stays private. The page also notes security challenges and mixed expectations about real-world benefits.

neural-processing-unit.title: AI accelerator (Wikipedia)
neural-processing-unit.notes: A neural processing unit is a form of AI accelerator: specialized hardware for artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads such as neural networks and computer vision. It can be a standalone chip or part of a CPU or GPU, and it either runs trained models for inference or trains models. Designs are often manycore or spatial and may use low-precision arithmetic, dataflow architectures or in-memory computing. Compared with general-purpose hardware they can be faster or more power-efficient; consumer NPUs are small and efficient, handle small models at reasonable speed and support low-bitwidth formats such as INT4, INT8, FP8 and FP16. Performance is often quoted in TOPS, typically counting INT8 operations. They appear in phones (Apple, Qualcomm, Samsung, Huawei, Google Tensor), in PCs from Apple, AMD and Intel, in GPUs with dedicated matrix units, and in cloud chips such as Google TPUs and AWS Trainium and Inferentia. Software support is fragmented across frameworks and vendor APIs such as CoreML, DirectML, ONNX, OpenVINO and Qualcomm SNPE, and the page calls the field an emerging technology without a dominant design.

new-commerce-experience.title: New commerce experience for license-based services (Partner Center)
new-commerce-experience.notes: The new commerce experience changes how Cloud Solution Provider partners buy and manage license-based subscriptions such as Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and Intune, without changing what can be bought. The Microsoft Customer Agreement and new commerce platform were introduced through CSP partners in 2019, and since 1 September 2024 all license-based subscription purchases are on new commerce, except six-year or five-year public sector legacy offers. Many subscriptions can be bought with monthly, annual or three-year terms and billed monthly, annually or up front. A subscription can only be cancelled in the first seven days of its term, and cancelling or reducing licences works differently from the legacy model; partners can schedule changes to take effect at the end of a term. Other points: offers are defined by product, SKU and availability (term) and addressed by a catalogItemId, pricing is defined per customer market and available through APIs, add-on purchases no longer depend on the base offer, and trials or paid SKUs can be converted with different quantities, terms and billing plans.

nis2.title: NIS2 Directive (European Commission)
nis2.notes: The NIS2 Directive (Directive 2022/2555) is the EU's unified legal framework for cybersecurity across 18 critical sectors. It keeps sectors from the first NIS Directive such as energy, transport, healthcare, finance, water and digital infrastructure and adds, among others, public electronic communications, more digital services, waste and wastewater management, critical product manufacturing, postal and courier services, public administration and space. Medium-sized and large entities in these sectors must take appropriate cybersecurity risk-management measures and notify national authorities of significant incidents. Top management is held accountable for non-compliance, which puts cybersecurity at board level. Member States must adopt a national cybersecurity strategy, strengthen national capabilities, and set rules for cooperation, information sharing, supervision and enforcement; EU structures include a CSIRTs network, EU-CyCLONe for large-scale crises and the NIS Cooperation Group. The directive entered into force in January 2023, had to be transposed by 17 October 2024 and repealed NIS1 from 18 October 2024. The page also mentions a Commission proposal of 20 January 2026 for targeted simplifying amendments. It does not state penalty amounts.

non-disclosure-agreement.title: Non-disclosure agreement (Wikipedia)
non-disclosure-agreement.notes: A non-disclosure agreement, also called a confidentiality agreement, is a contract between at least two parties that defines private information shared for a specific purpose and restricts who else may access it. It mainly protects non-public business information such as trade secrets. The page distinguishes unilateral NDAs, where only one side discloses, bilateral or mutual NDAs, where both disclose, and multilateral NDAs among three or more parties, which can replace several bilateral agreements. Typical clauses identify the parties, define covered information, set the disclosure period and the duration of confidentiality, list exclusions, require use only for the stated purpose and reasonable care, provide for return or destruction of materials at the end, and fix governing law and jurisdiction. Exceptions usually cover information the recipient already knew, learned lawfully elsewhere, or that becomes public, and disclosure under a subpoena. Overly broad NDAs may be unenforceable, and the page notes use of NDAs to silence harassment complaints, with laws in places such as the UK, Ireland and the US restricting such clauses.

nondeterministic-ai.title: Reproducible output with Azure OpenAI Chat Completions (Microsoft Learn)
nondeterministic-ai.notes: This Learn page explains that, by default, asking an Azure OpenAI chat model the same question several times usually gives different answers, so responses are nondeterministic, and it shows a preview feature for making them more consistent. The seed parameter accepts an integer; repeated requests with the same seed and the same other parameters, such as temperature and max_tokens, should return the same result, but the page stresses this is best effort and determinism is not guaranteed. The response also carries a system_fingerprint string that identifies the backend configuration; comparing it between calls shows when a backend change may alter outputs even with the same seed. In the page's example, three runs of one prompt at temperature 0.7 diverge more as the text gets longer without a seed; with seed 42 two runs are identical and the third starts the same and then diverges. Caveats: variability can still occur when seed and fingerprint match, larger max_tokens values tend to be less deterministic, and the feature was introduced with API version 2023-12-01-preview.

npm.title: npm (Wikipedia)
npm.notes: npm is a package manager for JavaScript and the default package manager for Node.js. It consists of a command-line client and an online registry of public and paid private packages, and it is maintained by npm, Inc., a GitHub subsidiary since GitHub bought it in March 2020. Isaac Z. Schlueter created it in 2010, with the first release on 12 January 2010. The registry hosts more than 3.1 million packages and has no vetting before publishing, so quality and security rely largely on user reports. A project lists its dependencies in package.json, ranges follow semantic versioning, package-lock.json records the exact resolved versions, npx runs packages without a permanent install, and npm audit, added in npm 6, checks for known vulnerabilities. The page recounts supply-chain incidents, including left-pad in 2016, event-stream in 2018, the sabotage of colors and faker in 2022 and phishing and worm attacks on popular packages in 2025. Alternatives such as pnpm, Yarn, Bun and Deno are compatible with the npm registry.

ntlm-relay-attack.title: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay (MITRE ATT&CK T1557.001)
ntlm-relay-attack.notes: MITRE ATT&CK describes name resolution poisoning and SMB relay as a sub-technique of adversary-in-the-middle for credential access on Windows. Hosts use local name resolution (LLMNR on UDP 5355, NBT-NS on UDP 137, mDNS on UDP 5353), and an adversary can answer those requests as if it were the requested host. If the victim then has to authenticate, its username and NTLMv2 hash are handed to the adversary, who can crack it offline. In the relay part, when an attacker sits in the authentication path or an automated credentialed scan authenticates to an attacker-controlled system, NTLMv1 or v2 authentication can be intercepted and relayed to a target to access it and execute code; the captured authentication can also be carried into other protocols such as LDAP, MSSQL and HTTP. Tools named include Responder, Metasploit and Impacket's ntlmrelayx. Mitigations listed are disabling LLMNR, mDNS and NetBIOS where not needed, blocking that traffic with host-based software, network intrusion prevention, segmentation, and the explicit note that enabling SMB signing can stop NTLMv2 relay attacks.

nvidia-omniverse.title: Nvidia Omniverse (Wikipedia)
nvidia-omniverse.notes: This Wikipedia article is a short stub that describes NVIDIA Omniverse as a real-time 3D graphics collaboration platform created by NVIDIA. It has been used in visual effects and in digital-twin industrial simulation, and it makes extensive use of the Universal Scene Description format. The page mentions support for third-party connectors to computer-aided design tools: an academic project built a connector between Omniverse and the open-source CAD system FreeCAD, giving collaborative access to CAD geometry through the Omniverse Nucleus server and extending use beyond media and entertainment. The cited sources point to a few milestones, namely integrations with Blender and Adobe in 2021, NVIDIA's metaverse strategy centred on Omniverse in 2021, an expansion toward the consumer internet in 2022 and the FreeCAD connector paper in 2025. The article does not cover pricing, licensing, supported platforms or a detailed feature list, and it does not mention Microsoft or Fabric.

nvme.title: NVM Express (Wikipedia)
nvme.notes: NVM Express (NVMe) is an open logical-device interface specification for accessing non-volatile storage, usually SSDs attached over PCI Express, maintained by NVM Express, Inc. The controller logic lives on the storage device, and NVMe is designed to exploit the low latency and internal parallelism of solid-state storage. Compared with AHCI, which has a single command queue of 32 commands, NVMe supports up to 65,535 queues each holding up to 65,536 commands, needs no locking to issue commands, supports up to 2,048 MSI-X interrupts and offers full-duplex transfer and a Host Memory Buffer. Form factors include add-in cards, U.2, U.3, M.2 (the most common consumer format) and CFexpress, and NVMe over Fabrics carries the protocol over transports such as Fibre Channel, TCP, RoCE and InfiniBand. Version 1.0 was released on 1 March 2011, version 2.0 in 2021 as a rearchitected set of specifications adding features such as Zoned Namespaces, and the page lists 2.4 as the latest. Samsung announced the first NVMe drive in July 2013, and Linux has supported NVMe since kernel 3.3.

nx.title: Intro to Nx (Nx documentation)
nx.notes: Nx is described as a build system for JavaScript and TypeScript monorepos, with plugins that extend it to other languages, aimed at helping teams develop faster and keep CI fast as the codebase grows. It targets problems such as slow builds and tests, complex task pipelines, flaky CI and architectural erosion. Nx runs tasks in dependency order and in parallel where possible, caches task results so unchanged work is not repeated (local caching is part of Nx Core, remote caching comes with Nx Cloud), and builds project and task graphs that also support module boundary rules against unwanted dependencies. Plugins add generators, auto-configured projects and tasks and dependency detection for technologies such as Angular, React, Vue, Node.js, Java and .NET. Nx Cloud is the paid CI layer, with remote caching, distributed task execution, task splitting, self-healing CI and flaky-test handling; the page quotes vendor performance figures for its private beta. The docs also cover Nx Release for versioning, changelogs and publishing, plus enterprise features such as conformance rules and code owners. The meta description says it serves monorepos and polyrepos.

ollama.title: ollama/ollama (GitHub repository)
ollama.notes: The repository README presents Ollama as a way to run open models locally or in the cloud, with the project licensed under MIT. It is built on the llama.cpp project and lets users start a model from a terminal command such as ollama run followed by a model name, with a model library at ollama.com. Ollama exposes a REST API on a local endpoint (port 11434, for example the chat endpoint) for running and managing models, and official Python and JavaScript client libraries exist. An ollama launch command starts supported integrations, and the README lists many community projects such as chat interfaces, editor plugins, SDKs, retrieval tools and observability tools. Installation is covered for macOS, Windows and Linux through install scripts or installers, and as an official Docker image, with package managers like Homebrew listed as well. Documentation covers the command line, the REST API, importing models, the Modelfile format and building from source. The page does not state hardware requirements or pricing for the cloud option.

one-stop-shop-vat.title: VAT One Stop Shop (European Commission)
one-stop-shop-vat.notes: The One Stop Shop (OSS) grew out of the mini One Stop Shop of 2015 and was expanded on 1 July 2021 to cover more supplies. It offers three optional schemes: the non-Union scheme for businesses without an establishment in the EU, the Union scheme (for EU-established businesses, and for certain goods supplies by non-EU businesses) and the import scheme for low-value imported goods of up to EUR 150 per consignment. A business registers in one Member State, its Member State of identification, and files electronic OSS VAT returns there, quarterly for the non-Union and Union schemes and monthly for the import scheme. That state passes returns and VAT on to the Member States of consumption. OSS returns are additional and do not replace regular domestic VAT returns, and opting in covers all relevant supplies to consumers in all Member States. Marketplaces can be treated as deemed suppliers, and the import scheme uses intermediaries for non-EU sellers. A EUR 10,000 annual threshold for cross-border B2C supplies keeps VAT in the home state below it. The page does not address deduction of input VAT.

onedrive-selective-sync.title: Choose which OneDrive folders you want to sync on Windows or macOS (Microsoft Support)
onedrive-selective-sync.notes: This support article explains how to select which OneDrive folders are kept on a Windows or macOS computer so that only important files are available offline. On Windows the path is OneDrive settings, Account tab, Choose folders, where you clear the folders you do not want on the device. Unchecking a folder that currently syncs removes it from the computer, while the folder and its contents stay in OneDrive online. Only folders that already exist in OneDrive can be checked or unchecked, so folders from external sources such as a USB drive cannot be added. Documents, Desktop, Pictures and the Personal Vault folder cannot be unchecked because the PC depends on them. The choices are specific to each computer and each account, and the OneDrive web and mobile apps always show all folders regardless of sync settings. The excerpt available to the summary contained only the Windows steps, not the macOS ones.

onedrive-sync-engine.title: How the OneDrive sync app works (Microsoft Learn)
onedrive-sync-engine.notes: This conceptual Learn page for admins explains how the OneDrive sync app detects and transfers changes. Instead of the older Groove.exe sync client, which polled on a schedule and caused system lag, the app relies on Windows Push Notification Services to hear about changes in Microsoft 365 in real time. A notification places the change in an internal server changes queue, processed in the order received; metadata changes such as renames and deletes are handled immediately, and content downloads open a dedicated session. For uploads, items under 8 MB go in a single HTTPS request, while items of 8 MB or more are split into chunks and sent one by one through a Background Intelligent Transfer Service session; other changes are batched. Office 2016 and 2019 files are synced in coordination with the Office apps, so the desktop app handles the sync if it is running. File chunks are stored in several Azure containers with separate keys, and a master key protects each chunk key. The page does not mention differential sync of changed bytes.

openfga.title: What is OpenFGA? (OpenFGA documentation)
openfga.notes: OpenFGA is described as a scalable, open source authorization system for developers, owned by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. It is inspired by Google's internal authorization system Zanzibar and uses relationship-based access control, which makes role-based access control easy to implement and adds capabilities toward attribute-based access control through contextual tuples and conditional relationship tuples. The claimed benefits are that authorization logic lives outside application code and is easier to write, change and audit, that teams can standardize on one solution, that decisions and audit logs are centralized and that policies are easier to evolve. Features named on the page include stores that separate environments or use cases, SDKs for Java, .NET, JavaScript, Go and Python, APIs over HTTP and gRPC, Postgres, MySQL or SQLite as production datastores plus an in-memory store for testing, a command-line tool, GitHub Actions for testing and deploying models, a VS Code extension, Helm charts and OpenTelemetry support. It can also run as a library inside a Go service. The page leaves details of modeling and check requests to linked documentation.

openusd.title: Universal Scene Description (Wikipedia)
openusd.notes: Universal Scene Description (USD) is a framework and file format family (.usd, .usda, .usdc and .usdz) for exchanging 3D computer graphics data, with emphasis on collaboration, non-destructive editing and support for several views and opinions about the data. Pixar developed it and first published it as open source in 2016 under a modified Apache licence. On 1 August 2023 Pixar, Adobe, Apple, Autodesk and Nvidia announced the Alliance for OpenUSD with the Joint Development Foundation of the Linux Foundation, aiming to promote standardization and growth of the technology. USDZ is the variant associated with Apple, supported through Reality Composer Pro and SceneKit. The page says USD is used in visual effects, architecture, design, robotics, CAD and rendering, and lists adopters including Adobe Substance 3D, Autodesk tools such as Maya and 3ds Max, Blender (import and export since version 4.0), Cinema 4D, Houdini, Nvidia Omniverse, Unreal Engine (importer in beta) and Vectorworks.

organizational-unit.title: Delegating administration by using OU objects (Windows Server, Microsoft Learn)
organizational-unit.notes: This Learn page treats organizational units in Active Directory Domain Services as containers for directory objects such as users and computers, and focuses on their use for delegating administration. Delegation takes three steps: put the people who will receive administrative rights into a group, put the objects to be controlled into an OU, and delegate the administrative tasks for that OU to the group. Permissions can be very fine grained; for example one group may have full control of all objects in an OU, another may only create, delete and manage user accounts, and a third may only reset passwords, and the permissions can be made inheritable to OUs below. Default OUs and containers created during AD DS installation are controlled by service administrators, who should keep that control; to delegate, create additional OUs, move objects into them and delegate those. The forest owner decides how much authority an OU owner gets, from managing all objects down to controlling one attribute of one object type, and creating an object implicitly gives the right to manipulate its attributes. The page is conceptual and has no step-by-step instructions.

orphaned-flows.title: Manage orphaned flows when the owner leaves the organization (Microsoft Learn)
orphaned-flows.notes: This troubleshooting article defines an orphaned flow as a Power Automate flow that no longer has a valid owner, typically because the owner has left the organization, and warns that such flows can fail if they use connections tied to that person's account. To find them in the Power Platform admin center, open the environment, go to Resources, then Flows, and look for flows with no owner in the Owners column (using Load more if the list is long). Reassignment in the admin center means selecting the flow, choosing Share and adding a new owner. For many flows the page recommends PowerShell with the Power Apps administration cmdlets: Get-AdminFlowOwnerRole shows owners, Set-AdminFlowOwnerRole adds a co-owner with the CanEdit role using the person's Entra object ID, and Get-AdminFlow with a CreatedBy filter lists everything a user created. A sample script loops through all flows in an environment and flags those where no owner or co-owner still exists in Microsoft Entra ID. The page also notes the deprecation of the Azure AD and MSOnline PowerShell modules in favour of Microsoft Graph PowerShell.

orphaned-workspace.title: Site ownership policies in SharePoint (Microsoft Learn)
orphaned-workspace.notes: Site ownership policies in SharePoint find sites that do not meet an organization's ownership requirements, notify responsible people and can take enforcement action. A policy sets the criteria, such as whether owners, admins or both count and how many are required, and runs in simulation mode (once, report only) or active mode (monthly, with reports, notifications and actions). Notifications can reach current owners, current admins, managers of previous owners or admins, and recently active members, and the categories add up rather than act as a fallback chain. Hard enforcement applies only to ownerless sites with zero owners: options are do nothing, make the site read-only after three monthly notices, or archive it through Microsoft 365 Archive after a mandatory read-only period. Only a tenant admin can unlock a read-only site or reactivate an archived one. Each run produces a downloadable CSV report. Limits include up to 10,000 URLs by CSV, exclusion lists of up to 100 entries, and exclusion of OneDrive, app catalog, root and home sites; SharePoint Advanced Management is a prerequisite. Manager information is deleted 30 days after a person leaves.

pac-validation.title: How to manage PAC Validation changes related to CVE-2024-26248 and CVE-2024-29056 (KB5037754)
pac-validation.notes: This Microsoft support article explains the Kerberos PAC Validation Protocol changes made by Windows updates from 9 April 2024. The Privilege Attribute Certificate is an extension to Kerberos service tickets that carries information about the user and their privileges. When a workstation performs PAC validation for an inbound Kerberos authentication, it sends a network ticket logon request to a domain controller, which asks the KDC to validate the PAC signatures of the service ticket; across domains the request travels over trusts and each domain controller filters the authorization data relevant to it. The fixed flaws are elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities in which a process on the workstation could spoof the signature and bypass checks added earlier through KB5020805. Rollout phases: compatibility mode from April 2024, enforced by default from January 2025, and full enforcement from April 2025 when the registry subkeys PacSignatureValidationLevel and CrossDomainFilteringLevel are removed. Installing updates alone does not fully protect, because partially updated environments stay vulnerable. The page also lists audit settings and event IDs such as 21, 22, 23, 5842 and 5843.

packml.title: PackML (Wikipedia)
packml.notes: PackML, short for Packaging Machine Language, is an industry technical standard for controlling packaging machines, intended to give all machines on a packaging line a common look and feel and consistent operation; its concepts are also used in converting, machine tools and robotics. It was created by OMAC, the Organization for Machine Automation and Control, together with the International Society of Automation, and OMAC became affiliated with ISA in 2005. PackML provides standardized machine states and operational flow, data for overall equipment effectiveness and root-cause analysis, and flexible recipe schemes with common SCADA or MES inputs. It extends the ISA-88 Part 1 state model concept, and ANSI/ISA-TR88.00.02 defines modes, states and data structures called PackTags, which give standard names to data elements and support machine-to-machine communication and exchange with MES and enterprise systems. The page traces the 2004 Make2Pack work, the harmonized TR88.00.02-2008 standard, and notes that PackML version 2 was memory-intensive for PLCs while version 3 fixed those problems. Control vendors such as Siemens, Rockwell, Mitsubishi and Beckhoff provide their own templates. The page does not list the individual states.

partner-development-manager.title: Microsoft partner program roles (AICloudPartners guide)
partner-development-manager.notes: This is a third-party partner guide, not Microsoft documentation, and it says its role details come from public Microsoft material and may change. It describes the Partner Development Manager as Microsoft's main relationship owner for a partner, sitting within Global Partner Solutions. The role manages partner strategy, programme enrolment, specialization qualification, co-sell pipeline and cross-workload business planning, and it connects partners to field sellers, technical resources and funding such as ECIF. According to the guide, PDMs are measured on partner-influenced Azure consumed revenue, co-sell pipeline value, specialization attainment, deal registrations and revenue targets, and each covers a small portfolio of about 5 to 15 strategic partners; only about 100 of more than 400,000 partners are said to get dedicated PDM support. Partners cannot request a PDM: Microsoft assigns one based on factors such as revenue contribution, specialization status, co-sell pipeline and strategic alignment, and earning an Advanced Specialization is called the most reliable trigger. Partners without a PDM usually work with Territory Channel Managers. The guide advises confirming current roles with a Microsoft contact.

passive-dns.title: What is passive DNS? A beginner's guide (Spamhaus)
passive-dns.notes: This vendor article describes passive DNS as a historical record of which IP addresses domain names resolved to over time. Without it, investigators cannot easily see past DNS records, because a change replaces the earlier value and the history is lost; with it, analysts can pivot from a domain to the IP addresses it used or from an IP to the domains that pointed to it. Records are created when a lookup misses the resolver's cache and an external authoritative server must answer; probes at the resolver capture the answer packets with a timestamp, and the data comes from trusted third parties such as hosting companies, enterprises and ISPs. Each entry holds the domain name, record type, record value and timestamp, and the article says no requestor IP addresses or user identities are stored, so there is no personal data. Uses named include investigating suspicious domains, spotting malicious infrastructure such as hostnames whose IP changes very often, tracking malware domains, analysing how domains relate and protecting brands from spoofed sites. Because only lookups that reached external servers are recorded, coverage is not complete. The page also advertises the vendor's own API and feeds.

password-writeback.title: Password writeback with self-service password reset (Microsoft Entra ID)
password-writeback.notes: Password writeback lets a password changed or reset in Microsoft Entra ID, for example through self-service password reset, be written back to on-premises Active Directory in real time. It is configured through Microsoft Entra Connect or Microsoft Entra Connect cloud sync and works with password hash synchronization, pass-through authentication and AD FS. The on-premises password policy (history, complexity, age, filters) is enforced before the password is committed, feedback to the user is immediate, and no inbound firewall rules are needed because traffic goes outbound over port 443 through an Azure Service Bus relay. The new password is encrypted with a public key created during setup, sent to a tenant-specific relay and set by the on-premises agent in the right forest; encryption uses a 2048-bit RSA key and 256-bit AES-GCM, and keys roll over every six months. Supported operations include end-user changes and resets from the portal and admin resets from the Entra admin center; resets through PowerShell or the Microsoft 365 admin center are not supported. Accounts in protected AD groups cannot be reset by the writeback service, and the feature is not supported with staged rollout enabled for a security group.

pdca-cycle.title: PDCA (Wikipedia)
pdca-cycle.notes: PDCA, or plan-do-check-act, is an iterative four-step method for improving processes and products. In Plan, objectives and the processes needed to reach them are set; in Do, the plan is carried out; in Check, the data and results from the Do phase are compared with the expected outcomes; and in Act, sometimes called adjust, problems and root causes are addressed and instructions, standards or goals are updated, and recurring issues show that the action was not effective. The page traces the idea to Walter Shewhart at Bell Laboratories in the 1920s and to W. Edwards Deming, who modified it in the 1940s, applied it to management in Japan in the 1950s and preferred the term Study, giving PDSA. Variants include OPDCA, which adds an initial Observe step. Each cycle builds on the last, forming a spiral of growing knowledge, and the method supports both large breakthrough changes and frequent small kaizen improvements. Uses named include manufacturing, healthcare, education and services, and related frameworks include DMAIC, Six Sigma and lean manufacturing.

pegging.title: Net requirements and pegging information (Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management)
pegging.notes: In Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management, pegging is the link between each requirement and the supply that covers it, or between each supply and the demand it fulfils. Master planning generates these links, and the Net requirements page shows them in a Pegging FastTab so planners can see how existing supply covers demand and why specific supply was created. Each pegging row shows a reference, a requirement quantity and a covered quantity. In the page's example, a sales order for 25 units is covered by 10 units on hand and a planned purchase order for 15 units, so the planned order exists only for the part that stock did not cover. Negative requirement quantities are demand and positive ones are supply. Pegging and net requirements reflect only the latest master planning run, so changes appear after planning is run again for the item, and the correct master plan must be selected in the Plan field first. The page can be opened from the product, a sales order line or a planned order, and safety stock does not appear on it.

per-tenant-extension.title: Extension types and scope (Dynamics 365 Business Central, Microsoft Learn)
per-tenant-extension.notes: This Learn page distinguishes per-tenant extensions from Marketplace apps in Business Central. A per-tenant extension is unique per environment, identified by id, version and the target environment; the same id and version can be deployed with different content to several environments, though that adds management overhead. The customer controls when to publish, install, upgrade, uninstall or unpublish it and can force a sync, and it may depend on global apps, other per-tenant extensions or dev extensions. It is installed by uploading the .app file in the Business Central admin center (the recommended route) or from the Extension Management page; the in-product upload and the Automation API upload endpoint are deprecated and slated for removal in 2027 release wave 1. A Marketplace app counts as a global app, published by Microsoft or a publisher and identified by id and version only, so its publishing timing is outside the customer's control. Production upgrades keep per-tenant extensions unless they block the upgrade during the enforced update period, and a global app and a per-tenant extension cannot share the same id.

permission-inheritance.title: What is permissions inheritance? (SharePoint, Microsoft Learn)
permission-inheritance.notes: Permissions inheritance in SharePoint means that an element's permission settings pass down to its children: sites inherit from the root site of the site collection, and libraries inherit from the site that contains them. An administrator assigns a permission once and it applies to every site, list, library, folder and item below it, which reduces complexity and security management time; by default sites inherit from their parent site. Inheritance flows top-down, and an object whose inheritance is broken still acts as a parent for its own items. When inheritance is broken, the child starts with a copy of the parent's permissions, can then be changed independently without affecting the parent, and can resume inheritance later; this can be done at any level. Sharing actions on an item that has children push the change down once to all children, including those with broken inheritance. The page advises against breaking inheritance unless necessary because it increases administrative complexity, suggests using built-in SharePoint groups for communication sites and the Microsoft 365 group for team sites, and grouping sensitive content so inheritance needs to be broken only once.

permissions-on-demand.title: Create or approve a request for permissions (Microsoft Entra Permissions Management, archived)
permissions-on-demand.notes: This archived Learn how-to describes privilege-on-demand requests in the Remediation dashboard of Microsoft Entra Permissions Management. A notice at the top states that the product could no longer be purchased from 1 April 2025 and was retired on 1 November 2025 with support discontinued. Supported clouds were AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform. A requester opens Remediation, My Requests, New Request, chooses the authorization system and accounts, and selects a role (for SAML users) or policies or tasks (for local users); for AWS a scope page allows choosing resources, optional request conditions and an Allow or Deny effect. On the confirmation page the requester adds a summary, an optional note for the approver and a schedule: ASAP, once with a date and duration, daily, weekly or monthly, with listed time limits such as 24 hours for ASAP and 2,160 hours (90 days) for once. Approvers open Pending Requests and choose Approve or Reject with an optional note. Requests are pending, approved or processed. The page does not describe expiry or revocation in detail.

persona.title: Persona (user experience) (Wikipedia)
persona.notes: A persona is a semi-fictional representation of a typical customer segment or end user that turns statistical and qualitative data into a relatable profile with a name and personality. Personas are used in user-centred design, marketing and software development to understand users' goals, desires and limitations. Alan Cooper is credited with proposing the user persona in software design, and his 1999 book The Inmates Are Running the Asylum popularized designing for single archetypal users. Personas are usually synthesized from interviews or surveys and written as short profiles with behaviour patterns, goals, skills, attitudes and a few invented personal details; data-driven personas use methods such as clustering and factor analysis, and hybrid personas combine quantitative and qualitative input. Claimed benefits are a shared understanding of users, easier feature prioritization, empathy, less self-referential design and avoiding the elastic user whom stakeholders define to suit themselves. Criticism is that personas are fictional and hard to validate, may reinforce stereotypes, rest on mostly anecdotal evidence, and proto-personas based on assumptions are often confused with research-based ones.

pester.title: Pester quick start (Pester documentation)
pester.notes: Pester is a testing and mocking framework for PowerShell, used mainly for unit and integration tests but also for validating environments, deployments and database configurations. Test files follow the *.Tests.ps1 naming convention, and tests can cover functions, cmdlets, modules and scripts. Installation is Install-Module Pester followed by Import-Module Pester to confirm the version, which the page shows as 6.1.0. The syntax uses Describe to group tests (often named after the function under test), Context to group by aspect, It for an individual test and Should to assert a condition, such as comparing a count with an expected value; BeforeAll runs once for shared setup such as dot-sourcing the function from its own file, and AfterAll, BeforeEach and AfterEach run at other points. Mock replaces the behaviour of commands inside the code under test and is covered in a separate guide. Tests run with Invoke-Pester, and Output Detailed lists every test. Pester works locally and inside Visual Studio Code, can run in a build script in a CI pipeline and can produce code coverage and test result files for CI reporting.

pkce.title: RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients
pkce.notes: RFC 7636, a Proposed Standard from September 2015 by Sakimura, Bradley and Agarwal, extends the OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant to protect public clients such as native mobile and desktop apps against authorization code interception. The attack works when a malicious app registers the same custom redirect scheme and captures the code; client secrets in app binaries cannot be kept confidential, so they do not help. PKCE has the client create a one-time secret for each authorization request and prove it when redeeming the code. The secret is the code_verifier, a high-entropy random string of 43 to 128 characters. The client sends a code_challenge derived from it plus the code_challenge_method, S256 (the Base64url-encoded SHA-256 hash of the verifier) or plain (the verifier itself). S256 is mandatory for servers to implement and must be used by clients whenever possible, while plain should not be used in new implementations; clients must not fall back to plain after an S256 failure. The server binds the challenge to the issued code, and at the token request it hashes the presented verifier and compares it, returning invalid_grant on mismatch. The RFC also creates an IANA registry for challenge methods.

plan-designer.title: Plans in Power Apps (Microsoft Learn)
plan-designer.notes: The Learn page documents Plans in Power Apps, a copilot-first tool for quickly creating business solutions. The maker describes a business use case in natural language and can optionally add images such as business process flows or screenshots of legacy apps; Plans then generates a complete Power Platform solution tailored to that input. The generated solution can include Microsoft Dataverse tables, canvas apps, model-driven apps, Power Pages sites, Power Automate flows and Copilot Studio agents. Requirements are an environment with a Dataverse database, Copilot features enabled and an eligible locale; if prerequisites are not met and developer environments are available, the maker is routed to their own developer environment. Plans is described as generally available and enabled by default, can only be turned off by a tenant administrator through Microsoft Support, and availability depends on region. System administrators, system customizers and environment makers can use it, and custom security roles need specific privileges on tables such as Plan, Entity and Solution. The page states no quotas or limits on images or generated output.

pnp-core-sdk.title: PnP Core SDK (PnP community documentation)
pnp-core-sdk.notes: The PnP Core SDK is described as a modern .NET SDK that provides a unified object model for working with SharePoint Online and Microsoft Teams, independent of the underlying APIs it calls. Its first focus is SharePoint Online and Teams developers, and other Microsoft 365 workloads may be added if the community asks for them. It targets modern .NET and is currently a dependency of PnP Framework, the older library built on .NET Framework that has been used in production for years; the maintainers plan to deprecate PnP Framework eventually and make the Core SDK the main library for Microsoft 365 work. It is open source and community provided, with no Microsoft SLA or direct Microsoft support; issues go through the GitHub issue list. Because it is a .NET Standard library, samples can target Windows, macOS, Linux, mobile and Blazor. Contribution guidance asks for tests, discussion of planned work first, avoidance of style-only or large unannounced pull requests, and only code the contributor wrote. The introduction page does not discuss a graph-first approach, fluent API or throttling handling.

pnp-modern-search.title: PnP Modern Search (project documentation)
pnp-modern-search.notes: PnP Modern Search v4 is a set of SharePoint Online modern web parts for building search-based experiences without lengthy setup, aimed at super users, webmasters and developers. It has four web parts: Search Results retrieves data from a data source and renders it in a chosen layout, Search Filters refines results, Search Verticals browses data as separate tabs from several data sources, and Search Box sends free-text queries to results web parts. The project began in 2017 as a successor to classic search web parts. Version 3 was stable and included protections against JavaScript and CSS injection that many enterprises relied on; v4 was rebuilt because Microsoft's search APIs are moving from SharePoint to Microsoft Graph, and it allows more extensibility through web components. Extension points include custom layouts, web components, Handlebars helpers and partials, Adaptive Cards action handlers, query modifiers, data sources and suggestion providers. Supported browsers are Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Brave; Internet Explorer 11 is not explicitly supported. Problems are reported through the GitHub issue list, and v4 was created by Franck Cornu from a fork of the Modern Data Visualizer.

pnp-react-controls.title: PnP SPFx React Controls (project documentation)
pnp-react-controls.notes: This is the documentation home for a library of reusable React controls for SharePoint Framework solutions, delivered as the npm package @pnp/spfx-controls-react and used in web parts and extensions. Controls fall into groups: layout and display (Accordion, Carousel, GridLayout, Pagination, Map, RichText), charts built on a chart control, pickers (PeoplePicker, TaxonomyPicker, ModernTaxonomyPicker, FilePicker, FolderPicker, ListPicker, SitePicker, TeamPicker, DateTimePicker and more), lists and data (ListView, TreeView, FieldCollectionData, DynamicForm, UploadFiles), theming providers, Microsoft Teams helpers and other items such as ShareDialog and SecurityTrimmedControl, plus a set of field renderers for field customizers. Installation is npm install with save and save-exact. Version 3 is the actively maintained line, targeting SPFx 1.13 and Fluent UI 7.174.1 for SharePoint Online; version 2 targets SPFx 1.11.0 and is advised to be upgraded, and version 1 targets SPFx 1.3.0 for SharePoint 2016 and 2019 on-premises. All controls collect basic usage telemetry that can be disabled from version 1.17.0 with an opt-out call.

policy-decision-point.title: XACML (Wikipedia)
policy-decision-point.notes: In the XACML access-control architecture, the Policy Decision Point is the central, environment-independent component that evaluates an authorization request against policies and returns the final decision: Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate. It receives the request from the Policy Enforcement Point, retrieves policies from the Policy Retrieval Point (managed by a Policy Administration Point), and pulls attribute values from Policy Information Points when needed. XACML is an OASIS standard that defines a declarative, fine-grained, attribute-based policy language, an architecture and a processing model, used mainly for attribute-based access control and also usable for role-based control. Policies are organized as policy sets, policies and rules, with targets deciding applicability, boolean conditions inside rules, and combining algorithms that resolve conflicts between results. Obligations are actions the enforcement point must carry out, while advice may be ignored. The specification covers the policy language the decision point consumes, not how a decision point is built. The page names Open Policy Agent as an open-source decision point, notes its Rego language cannot always express XACML policies, and lists versions 1.0 (2003) to 3.0 (2013).

policy-enforcement-point.title: XACML (Wikipedia)
policy-enforcement-point.notes: In the XACML architecture, the Policy Enforcement Point is the component that intercepts a user's access request to a resource, turns it into an authorization request, asks the Policy Decision Point for a decision and then enforces the answer on the original request. The flow described is: the user requests access and the enforcement point intercepts it, converts it into a XACML request and sends it to the decision point, which evaluates policies obtained from the retrieval point (managed by the administration point) and may fetch attributes from information points; it returns Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate, and the enforcement point carries it out. The enforcement point must also perform any obligations attached to the decision, such as logging, while advice is optional for it. XACML is an OASIS attribute-based access control standard, and the page notes it complements rather than replaces protocols such as SAML, which carries identity information, and OAuth, which handles delegated authorization. XACML itself does not handle user approval, delegation of consent or password management. The page does not discuss synchronous evaluation before a state change commits.

power-automate-process-license.title: Power Automate licensing types (Microsoft Learn)
power-automate-process-license.notes: The Process license is a paid capacity license for Power Automate that attaches to automations rather than to people: cloud flows and machines. Assigned to a cloud flow, it gives higher action limits and premium and custom connectors regardless of the licence of the user who owns or triggers the flow, and the flow must be in a solution first. Allocated to a machine, it becomes an unattended bot that runs one desktop flow at a time, and for parallel unattended runs one licence is needed per concurrent run. Each Process licence allows up to 250,000 actions per day, sized as actions per run multiplied by runs per day, and the comparison table lists 5,000 AI Builder credits per month, 50 MB of Dataverse database storage and 200 MB of file storage per licence, with standard, premium and custom connectors, business process flows and on-premises gateways included. Attended and hosted RPA and process mining are not included. Licences can be stacked on one flow or shared across a flow group. The page says a Process licence is not meant to replace user licences, and triggering desktop flows from cloud flows still needs a Power Automate Premium user. It does not mention the former name or a price.

power-automate-run-history.title: Limits and configuration in Power Automate (Microsoft Learn)
power-automate-run-history.notes: The limits page for Power Automate sets a 30-day limit on run retention in storage, measured from the run's start time; cloud flow run history is therefore only kept for that period. The same table sets a 30-day maximum run duration, which includes flows with pending steps such as approvals, whose pending steps time out after 30 days. Run history is also subject to throughput limits: reading raw inputs and outputs from a run's history counts toward read-call limits per five minutes, and the amount of data read or written to run history is capped per five minutes and per 24 hours, with different values for the Low, Medium and High profiles and temporarily higher values during a transition period. The page adds that if a test of a cloud flow runs longer than 10 minutes, a timeout message may appear while the flow keeps running in the background, and that turning off a flow stops new runs while in-progress and pending runs continue. It does not say what happens to history after the retention period, and it does not call run history an audit record, so that framing comes from elsewhere.
